notes.decision: Translated 'the New Man' (Pauline καινὸς ἄνθρωπος). Analysis: ⲣⲙ̄- ('man of') + ⲛ̄- (genitive) + ⲃⲣ̄ⲡⲉ (Lyc. for ⲃⲣ̄ⲣⲉ 'new'). Confirmed by antithesis with ⲡⲣⲙⲛⲉⲥ in line 15 = 'the Old Man' (παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος). The kephalaion is structured around this Pauline-Manichaean anthropological dyad: the New Man's five faculties produce virtues; the Old Man's same faculties are corrupted by Sin. NOTE: this corrects the accumulated-vocab gloss of ⲡⲣⲙⲛⲉⲥ as 'the Ancient One' for this context — here it is the Pauline 'old man.'

Translated 'the Old Man' (παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος, Pauline anthropology). The accumulated vocabulary glossed this as 'the Ancient One' from a different cosmological context. Here, the strict antithesis with ⲡⲣⲙ̄ⲛ̄ⲃⲣ̄ⲡⲉ ('the New Man') and the description of being 'bound' in lust, foolishness, and the spirit of darkness (lines 15-19) confirm the anthropological-soteriological reading: this is the unredeemed pre-conversion self, whose five faculties are corrupted.

Translated 'is mingled inward.' Most likely a Lycopolitan reflex of ⲧⲱⲧ qualitative ⲧⲏⲧ 'be joined/mingled' with prosthetic/intensive ⲁ-. Recurs in line 24 of Sin mingled inward with the Mind of Light. Captures the Manichaean cosmological-anthropological motif of dark and light substances commingled within the body.

ϣⲁϩ- = Lycopolitan habitual ϣⲁϥ- 'he is wont to.' Translated as 'he places' / 'he purifies' for English fluency, though the habitual aspect is implied throughout the description of the New Man's regular practice.

Translated 'salt' (Lyc. ⲍ for ϩ; ϩⲙⲟⲩ = salt). Read alongside the preceding 'bitter words' as a gustatory-correspondence pair describing the corrupted speech of the Old Man under Sin's influence. Alternative reading 'blessing' (ⲥⲙⲟⲩ with ⲥ→ⲍ) is possible but less phonetically regular.
Translated 'time' (occasion). Standard Coptic ⲥⲁⲡ/ⲥⲏⲩ. The construction ⲟⲩⲛ ⲥⲁⲡ ⲉϣⲁⲣⲉ X = 'there is a time when X' introduces a habitual scenario.

Translated 'the separation — out of his hand.' ⲡⲧⲱⲣϫ̄ = 'separation, division' (Sah. ⲡⲱⲣϫ̄). ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧϩ̄ = 'from his hand' = 'from him.' The phrase signals Sin's act of severing the man from truth, throwing him into double-mindedness (ⲙⲛⲧϩⲏⲧⲥⲛⲉⲩ).

Translated 'this is the manner.' Likely a Lycopolitan demonstrative-form of ⲧⲛⲟ/ⲡⲛⲟ 'manner, way' (in accumulated vocabulary). Functions as the resumptive 'this manner' formula introducing the summary clause.
